<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Multimodal geometry reasoning requires models to jointly understand visual diagrams and perform
structured symbolic inference, yet current vision–language models struggle with complex geometric
constructions due to limited training data and weak visual–symbolic alignment.
We propose a pipeline for synthesizing complex multimodal geometry problems from scratch and construct
a dataset named <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GeoCode</span>, which decouples problem generation into symbolic seed construction,
grounded instantiation with verification, and code-based diagram rendering, ensuring consistency across
structure, text, reasoning, and images.
Leveraging the plotting code provided in GeoCode, we further introduce code prediction as an explicit
alignment objective, transforming visual understanding into a supervised structured prediction task.
GeoCode exhibits substantially higher structural complexity and reasoning difficulty than existing benchmarks,
while maintaining mathematical correctness through multi-stage validation.
Extensive experiments show that models trained on GeoCode achieve consistent improvements on multiple geometry
benchmarks, demonstrating both the effectiveness of the dataset and the proposed alignment strategy.
The code will be available at <a href="https://github.com/would1920/GeoCode" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/would1920/GeoCode</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Geometry reasoning has long been regarded as a core testbed for multimodal intelligence.
Unlike natural image understanding or general visual question answering, geometry problems
require precise visual perception, structured symbolic representations, and multi-step logical
reasoning to jointly support a verifiable conclusion. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite></p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18745v1/figure1.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/216;" width="476" height="216" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Motivation of our work.<span id="S1.F1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> We address the limitations of implicit visual–symbolic alignment and low structural diversity and low problem difficulty in current geometry datasets by synthesizing problems from scratch and supervising models with plotting code for explicit structural grounding.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Recent advances in vision–language models (VLMs)<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> have led to notable progress on basic
geometry-related benchmarks<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>.
However, when faced with problems involving complex constructions, dense relational
constraints, and long-chain reasoning, current models still exhibit substantial limitations,
particularly in their ability to recover geometric structure from diagrams and to
maintain consistency across intermediate reasoning steps<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">From a problem-solving perspective, multimodal geometry reasoning is commonly decomposed into two stages:
(1) visual–symbolic alignment, which recovers structured geometric entities and relational constraints from diagrams, and
(2) symbolic reasoning, which performs deductive inference under joint visual and textual conditions.
Recent advances in formal geometry solvers show that, when accurate symbolic representations are available, purely symbolic systems can solve problems approaching International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO) level without any visual input <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>, indicating that long-horizon geometric deduction itself is largely tractable.
In contrast, multimodal models must additionally infer symbolic structure from visual diagrams, and empirical evaluations on geometry benchmarks reveal persistent failures in robust structure recovery and intermediate-step consistency under complex constructions and dense relational constraints <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>.
This suggests that the dominant bottleneck lies in converting visual layouts into faithful symbolic representations rather than in downstream logical inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Existing methods attempt to mitigate this gap through improved vision–language alignment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>, synthetic data generation with reasoning supervision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>, or solver-driven pipelines that ensure symbolic correctness <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>, achieving notable progress on standard benchmarks.
Nevertheless, two limitations remain: most datasets are generated via manual design or limited symbolic sampling, resulting in restricted structural diversity and insufficient reasoning depth, and alignment is typically supervised only at the level of answers or natural-language reasoning, leaving geometric structure recovery from diagrams weakly constrained and largely implicit.
Consequently, models may rely on linguistic correlations or dataset biases rather than explicitly reconstructing geometric relations from visual input.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Unlike general multimodal reasoning tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>, geometry possesses a distinctive advantage: its structures are both symbolically solvable and numerically verifiable via coordinate-based constructions, enabling strict validation of geometric consistency.
This property makes it feasible to synthesize geometry problems from scratch with correctness guarantees and to enforce cross-modal consistency among symbolic structures, language, reasoning traces, and rendered diagrams, an opportunity that remains underexploited in existing multimodal geometry datasets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by this observation, we propose a pipeline for synthesizing
multimodal geometry problems from scratch, and construct a dataset named GeoCode.
Our pipeline begins with symbolic geometric seeds constructed via dependency analysis
using systems such as AlphaGeometry, ensuring that each seed admits non-trivial deductive targets
at the symbolic level.
These structures are then instantiated by large language models, which propose concrete
numerical parameters, natural language problem statements, and reasoning traces.
To ground these textual specifications into explicit geometric configurations, a separate Coder
module generates meta code that constructs coordinate-level realizations of all
geometric entities.
Finally, we perform strict semantic and geometric validation, together with visual quality
filtering, to discard inconsistent or ill-posed samples.
As a result, each retained instance maintains strict consistency across symbolic structure,
textual description, reasoning process, and visual representation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond data generation, the availability of plotting code in <span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GeoCode</span> further enables a new alignment paradigm based on code-supervised diagram understanding.
Instead of supervising models only with answers or textual reasoning, we introduce plotting
code as an explicit supervision target.
Predicting plotting code requires models to reconstruct the full geometric structure
from images, including construction dependencies and spatial relations, effectively converting
visual understanding into a structured and verifiable prediction task.
This design makes geometric perception an explicit and supervised component of the learning
objective, rather than an implicit latent representation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Extensive experiments demonstrate that our synthesized dataset exhibits higher
structural complexity and reasoning difficulty than existing geometry benchmarks, and that
models trained on our data achieve consistent improvements across multiple public geometry
datasets, also under out-of-distribution evaluation.
Ablation studies further confirm the critical role of plotting-code supervision in strengthening
visual–symbolic alignment, showing clear advantages over text-only alignment.
We argue that geometric diagrams are inherently complete and representations of
structure, whereas language is unavoidably lossy and ambiguous; therefore, effective geometry
reasoning should be grounded in explicit structural representations rather than relying solely
on linguistic supervision.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p10" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose a pipeline to synthesize multimodal geometry problems from scratch, with verification across symbolic structure, language description, reasoning trace, and visual diagram.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We construct <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GeoCode</span>, an 18K multimodal geometry dataset with diagrams, solutions, and plotting code, while achieving significantly higher difficulty and structural complexity under strict correctness.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce plotting code as an explicit supervision target for cross-modal alignment, enabling structured learning of geometric relations from visual diagrams.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show consistent improvements on multiple public geometry benchmarks, including in out-of-distribution settings.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multimodal Large Language Models and Reasoning</span>
Recent years have witnessed rapid advances in large language models (LLMs), leading to strong performance across a wide range of reasoning tasks. The introduction of GPT-4<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite> and subsequent vision–language models<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> has further shifted the community’s focus toward multimodal understanding<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>, where extracting and integrating visual information becomes an essential capability. To enhance reasoning, many works adopt explicit intermediate supervision such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT)<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>, enabling models to generate multi-step reasoning traces. More recently, reinforcement learning based alignment methods, including PPO<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite> and GRPO<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>, have been widely applied to further optimize reasoning behaviors under task-specific objectives or preference feedback, yielding consistent improvements on complex reasoning benchmarks.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18745v1/figure2.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/268;" width="476" height="268" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S2.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of the data generation pipeline.<span id="S2.F2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Our framework factorizes synthesis into three verifiable stages: (1) Seed Generation for symbolic relational structures, (2) Instantiation for numerical grounding and meta-code generation, and (3) Visualization for diagram rendering and textual debiasing.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multimodal Geometry Problem Solving.</span>
Geometry problem solving is a challenging multimodal task that requires jointly understanding visual diagrams and performing structured symbolic reasoning. With the development of multimodal LLMs, MGPS has become an important testbed for evaluating visual–symbolic reasoning. Existing approaches mainly fall into three categories: alignment-oriented methods such as EAGLE<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite> and MAVIS<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> that enhance visual perception via staged vision–language alignment, data-centric methods such as R-CoT<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>, G-LLaVA<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>, and MathCoder-VL<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> that construct synthetic multimodal training data with reasoning traces, and solver-driven generation methods that leverage symbolic geometry solvers such as AlphaGeometry<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, with representative works including GeoGen<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite> and TrustGeoGen<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>.
However, two fundamental challenges remain. <em id="S2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">First</em>, the lack of large-scale, high-quality geometry datasets with sufficient structural complexity and strict cross-modal consistency limits models’ ability to learn long-range geometric dependencies and multi-step reasoning patterns. <em id="S2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Second</em>, effective visual–symbolic alignment mechanisms are still underexplored, as most methods supervise only final answers or textual reasoning without explicitly constraining geometric structure reconstruction from diagrams.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we present a generation pipeline for synthesizing complex multimodal geometry problems from scratch.
We first construct symbolic geometric structures and instantiate them with concrete metrics, and then render them into visual diagrams to ensure strict cross-modal consistency in Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Generation Pipeline ‣ 3 Method ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>.
Building on this pipeline, we further introduce plotting code as an explicit alignment target in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Plotting Code as Explicit Alignment ‣ 3 Method ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>, which supervises models to recover geometric structure directly from diagrams.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Generation Pipeline</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As illustrated in Fig. <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, our generation pipeline factorizes multimodal geometry problem synthesis into three modular and verifiable stages:
(i) symbolic seed generation for constructing relational structures,
(ii) grounded instantiation with semantic and geometric verification,
and (iii) visualization with textual debiasing.
This decomposition disentangles logical structure, metric realization, and perceptual presentation, enabling controllable synthesis while maintaining strict cross-modal alignment.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.1 </span>Seed Generation</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This stage focuses on constructing symbolic geometric structures without numerical grounding or linguistic formulation.
While random sampling and theorem provers are effective at exploring and validating relational configurations, assigning metric values that both satisfy constraints and yield pedagogically meaningful problems is considerably more difficult and error prone.
We therefore decouple structural discovery from metric instantiation, and restrict this stage to symbolic reasoning over geometric predicates.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Seed generation starts from random sampling of predicate sets, which specify relations such as incidence, parallelism, perpendicularity, and equality among abstract geometric entities.
These sampled predicates form candidate relational graphs, serving as hypotheses in the symbolic space.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Target Finder via Dependency Construction.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a predicate set <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> and a theorem library <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}</annotation></semantics></math>, we apply forward symbolic reasoning to derive all propositions that are logically implied by <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{D}(S)=\{\,p\mid S\vdash_{\mathcal{T}}p\,\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.170em" stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>S</mi><msub><mo>⊢</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi></msub><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}(S)=\{\,p\mid S\vdash_{\mathcal{T}}p\,\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">AlphaGeometry is used as the reasoning engine to construct dependency graphs, where nodes correspond to predicates and edges encode proof dependencies.
Each valid reasoning target is associated with a proof graph consisting of premises, intermediate steps, and a final conclusion.
This process determines whether the sampled structure admits non-trivial deductive chains rather than isolated or redundant constraints.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Filter and Selection.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Due to the stochastic nature of predicate sampling, many derived configurations are trivial, degenerate, or pedagogically uninformative.
We first discard cases that reduce to tautological or equivalent propositions.
For the remaining candidates, we characterize symbolic complexity using two complementary measures: the number of premises, reflecting structural breadth, and the number of proof steps, reflecting deductive depth.
We rank all candidates by each measure separately, retain the top <math id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> percentile under both rankings, and take their intersection as the final seed set.
This strategy biases selection toward problems that are simultaneously structurally rich and reasoning-intensive in the symbolic space.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">After template-based translation, each retained configuration is represented as <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Seed Data</span> consisting of (i) symbolic premises, (ii) ordered proof steps, and (iii) target conclusions.
Notably, these seeds specify only geometric structure and logical relations, and contain no numerical values or coordinate information.
They define abstract problem skeletons that will be grounded and verified in the subsequent instantiation stage.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.2 </span>Instantiation</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This stage maps abstract symbolic seeds into fully specified geometry problems with numerical grounding, natural language formulation, geometric constructions, and verified answers.
Concretely, instantiation produces problem statements, reasoning traces, final answers, and geometric construction programs that together define a complete problem instance.
To achieve this, we decompose instantiation into three functional components: an Instructor for problem realization, a Coder for geometric construction, and a two-stage verification mechanism for correctness control.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Instructor for Numerical Grounding and Reasoning Generation.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given Seed Data consisting of symbolic premises, proof structures, and target conclusions, we employ a reasoning-oriented language model as an <span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Instructor</span> to generate instantiated geometry problems.
The Instructor assigns concrete numerical values that satisfy all symbolic constraints (e.g., selecting Pythagorean triples for right triangles), translates formal predicates into natural language problem statements, and produces ordered reasoning traces together with final answers.
This process transforms abstract relational structures into solvable and pedagogically meaningful geometry questions while preserving all logical dependencies encoded in the seed.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Coder for Geometric Construction.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each instantiated problem, we further generate geometric <span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">meta code</span> using a separate <span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Coder</span> model.
Conditioned only on the problem statement, the Coder predicts a set of executable construction functions that compute coordinates of geometric entities through numerical and geometric computations.
These functions are executed in a sandbox environment and are parsed to recover two types of information: (i) concrete coordinates of all points, and (ii) structured drawing information, such as which points are connected by segments, which circles are drawn, and what symbolic annotations are present. 
By executing and parsing these construction functions, we obtain a complete geometric scene specification that supports both numerical verification and deterministic visualization.
Importantly, the Coder does not receive the reasoning trace or the final answer as input, preventing leakage of solution information into the geometric construction process.
This ensures that all geometric realizations are grounded solely in the textual problem description.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Two-stage Verification.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure correctness and consistency across modalities, we perform verification at both semantic and geometric levels.
<span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1) Semantic validation.</span> An independent language model evaluates whether the problem statement is logically coherent, whether the generated reasoning trace follows from the premises, and whether the stated answer is consistent with the reasoning.
<span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2) Geometric validation.</span> Using coordinates produced by executing the meta code, we numerically verify all declared constraints, including lengths, angles, parallelism, and perpendicularity, as well as the final answer when it involves metric quantities.
Samples that violate any semantic or geometric condition are discarded.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.3 </span>Visualization</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This stage transforms geometric constructions into visual diagrams and removes textual shortcuts that may undermine genuine multimodal reasoning.
It consists of two components: diagram rendering based on plotting code, and textual debiasing that enforces reliance on visual information.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Diagram Rendering.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">By executing and parsing the meta code, we obtain structured <span id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">plotting code</span>, including point coordinates and drawing specifications such as segments, circles, and annotations.
Using these two types of information, we render geometry diagrams with OpenCV, following standard textbook-style conventions to produce clean and unambiguous figures.
In practice, we observe that certain constructions may lead to severe visual overlap or near-degenerate layouts that hinder perception.
We therefore perform image-level quality checks and discard samples with excessive overlaps or ambiguous configurations, ensuring that retained diagrams are visually interpretable and suitable for learning.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18745v1/figure3.png" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/305;" width="381" height="305" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.F3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Plotting code as explicit alignment.<span id="S3.F3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Instead of relying on lossy linguistic descriptions, we utilize structured plotting code as an intermediate representation to couple visual perception with symbolic reasoning.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Textual Debiasing.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS3.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Previous studies have shown that models can achieve non-trivial performance on geometry tasks using text alone<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>, suggesting that textual descriptions may act as shortcuts that bypass visual reasoning.
Such behavior contradicts the goal of multimodal geometry understanding.
To mitigate this issue, we explicitly remove from the question all information that can be directly inferred from the diagram, such as relative positions, intersections, and marked equalities.
Moreover, we rewrite the reasoning traces to reflect interactions between visual observations and textual premises, rather than purely symbolic deductions.
As a result, solving the problem requires extracting geometric relations from the image instead of relying on redundant textual cues.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Plotting Code as Explicit Alignment</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Benefiting from our generation pipeline, each problem instance is associated not only with images, questions, and answers, but also with structured plotting code that explicitly describes the underlying geometric scene.
This additional supervision enables us to move beyond answer-level learning and directly supervise geometric perception.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Plotting code serves as a geometry-specific intermediate representation that can be deterministically rendered into diagrams and explicitly encodes geometric entities, constructions, and visual relations.
From this perspective, understanding a geometry problem naturally corresponds to recovering its plotting code from the input image.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Based on this observation, we train models to explicitly predict plotting code in addition to reasoning traces and final answers.
Given an input diagram and question, the model is supervised to first reconstruct the geometric scene in the form of plotting code, and then perform reasoning and answer prediction based on the recovered structure. 
This design makes visual understanding an explicit learning process rather than an implicit latent process.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Compared to answer-only or text-only supervision, plotting-code-based alignment enforces stronger coupling between visual perception and symbolic reasoning, which we empirically show to be critical for robust multimodal geometry reasoning.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18745v1/figure4.png" id="S3.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/125;" width="452" height="125" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S3.F4.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Exemplary data generation and model inference.<span id="S3.F4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> The left panel illustrates the end-to-end synthesis process: from Symbolic Seed to Template-based Translation, followed by the Numerical Question, its corresponding Plotting Code, the Debiased Problem statement, and the finally rendered Diagram. The right panel showcases a real-world Inference Example, demonstrating the model’s ability to perform structured reasoning and code-based grounding during testing.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we systematically evaluate the quality of the generated geometry problems and the effectiveness of the proposed alignment strategy.
We first describe the implementation and experimental settings in Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Implementation Details ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>.
We then analyze the structural complexity and difficulty of our GeoCode in Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Quality and Difficulty of GeoCode ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>.
Next, we evaluate how well models trained on our synthetic data transfer to public geometry benchmarks in Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Effectiveness on Test-mini and Public Benchmarks ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>.
Finally, we conduct ablation studies to examine the roles of different pipeline components and plotting-code alignment in Sections <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Ablation Study on Pipeline Components ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a> and <a href="#S4.SS5" title="4.5 Plotting Code Enables Stronger Visual Alignment ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Implementation Details</h3>

<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Pipeline Implementation.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use GenesisGeo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> for symbolic seed generation and structural selection.
Instantiation, reasoning trace generation, semantic validation, textual debiasing, and plotting-code generation are all performed by GPT-OSS-120B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>.
Diagrams are rendered using OpenCV, followed by image-based quality filtering with Qwen3-VL-32B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite> to remove visually ambiguous samples.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Training and Evaluation.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All models are trained using LLaMA-Factory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite> with Qwen3-VL-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct as backbones, using LoRA-based SFT for 2 epochs (learning rate <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\times 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>, warmup ratio 0.1).
For reinforcement learning, we adopt standard GRPO optimization via the Verl framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>, with learning rate <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\times 10^{-6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\times 10^{-6}</annotation></semantics></math>, clip ratio <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=0.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=0.2</annotation></semantics></math>, KL coefficient <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.01</annotation></semantics></math>, and 4 samples per prompt.
All evaluations use identical prompts, greedy decoding (<math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0</annotation></semantics></math>), exact-match normalization, and images resized to <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="224\times 224" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>224</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>224</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">224\times 224</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Quality and Difficulty of GeoCode</h3>

<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Data.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">GeoCode contains a total of 18k geometry problems, including 13k numerical solution problems and 5k proof-based problems.
For numerical problems, we randomly sample 2% of the data to form a held-out test-mini set, which is used for controlled difficulty analysis and comparison with standard benchmarks. All other experiments use disjoint training and test splits.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Correctness.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All generated samples are filtered by both semantic validation and coordinate geometric verification, ensuring consistency among symbolic relations, numerical constructions, and final answers.
To further assess potential residual errors beyond automatic checks, We conduct manual inspection on a random 1% subset of the generated data, and observe no incorrect or inconsistent cases.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Diversity.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze symbolic seeds to assess structural diversity. Overall, problems exhibit diverse combinations of geometric relations rather than single isolated constraints, and predicate usage follows a long-tailed distribution where frequent relations (e.g., perpendicularity, parallelism) coexist with less frequent but structurally important ones (e.g., cyclic and similarity constructions). This indicates that the dataset is not composed of repetitive templates but covers a wide range of geometric configurations.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">

<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Complexity.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze problem complexity from both structural and difficulty perspectives.
<span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1) Structure</span> We evaluate not only symbolic seeds but also the final rendered diagrams, computing statistics such as the average number of segments and annotated relations per problem. The distributions show that most problems involve multiple entities and constraints, indicating higher structural richness compared to commonly used training data, as summarized in <a href="#S4.T1" title="In Diversity. ‣ 4.2 Quality and Difficulty of GeoCode ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
<span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2) Difficulty</span> To assess problem difficulty and prove complexity is meaningful, we compare model performance on the test-mini set with several standard geometry benchmarks under identical evaluation protocols. As shown in <a href="#S4.T2" title="In Diversity. ‣ 4.2 Quality and Difficulty of GeoCode ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, test-mini exhibits higher difficulty, reflecting the non-trivial reasoning complexity of the generated problems. Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.2 Plotting Code as Explicit Alignment ‣ 3 Method ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> qualitatively demonstrates our dataset’s complexity and consistency, showcasing the full transition from seed to debiased problem, plotting code, and rendered diagram. More statistics can be found in Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Example Data from Our Pipeline ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<td id="S4.T5.3.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:10.0pt;padding-right:10.0pt;"><span id="S4.T5.3.2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">10,510</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T5.3.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T5.3.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding-left:10.0pt;padding-right:10.0pt;"><span id="S4.T5.3.3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Geometric verification</span></td>
<td id="S4.T5.3.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:10.0pt;padding-right:10.0pt;"><span id="S4.T5.3.3.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">4,171</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T5.3.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T5.3.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding-left:10.0pt;padding-right:10.0pt;"><span id="S4.T5.3.4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Plotting execution</span></td>
<td id="S4.T5.3.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:10.0pt;padding-right:10.0pt;"><span id="S4.T5.3.4.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">2,017</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T5.3.5" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T5.3.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding-left:10.0pt;padding-right:10.0pt;"><span id="S4.T5.3.5.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Image quality filter</span></td>
<td id="S4.T5.3.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:10.0pt;padding-right:10.0pt;"><span id="S4.T5.3.5.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">423</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T5.3.6" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T5.3.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:10.0pt;padding-right:10.0pt;"><span id="S4.T5.3.6.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Total rejected</span></td>
<td id="S4.T5.3.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:10.0pt;padding-right:10.0pt;"><span id="S4.T5.3.6.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">17,121</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T5.3.7" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T5.3.7.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:10.0pt;padding-right:10.0pt;"><span id="S4.T5.3.7.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Final retained</span></td>
<td id="S4.T5.3.7.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:10.0pt;padding-right:10.0pt;"><span id="S4.T5.3.7.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">18,176</span></td></tr>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>Detailed rejection statistics during the multi-stage validation pipeline. </figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation on Test-mini.</span>
We first evaluate models trained on GeoCode on Test-mini, a held-out subset constructed from unseen symbolic seeds and instantiations, which exhibits higher structural complexity and denser geometric constraints than standard benchmarks.
To more directly assess the effectiveness of the generated data, we adopt a two-stage training scheme with SFT followed by GRPO. Notably, during the GRPO stage, we apply rewards only on answer correctness and output format, without supervising intermediate reasoning traces or plotting code, so that improvements can be attributed to data quality rather than additional structured supervision.
As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Complexity. ‣ 4.2 Quality and Difficulty of GeoCode ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, both backbones benefit substantially from SFT and further improve with GRPO. For Qwen3-VL-Instruct, accuracy increases from 17.9% to 26.5% after SFT and further to 37.7% after GRPO, while Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct improves from 4.5% to 13.1% and then to 20.5%, respectively.
These consistent gains indicate that GeoCode provides strong and stable learning signals even when reinforcement learning is driven solely by final-answer supervision, demonstrating the intrinsic effectiveness of the generated problems.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Transfer to Public Geometry Benchmarks.</span>
To evaluate out-of-distribution generalization, we further assess models on multiple public benchmarks, including Geometry3K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>, MathVerse <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>, MathVista <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>, GeoQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>, and OlympiadBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>. For general vision–math benchmarks, we report results only on plane-geometry subsets.
As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Diversity. ‣ 4.2 Quality and Difficulty of GeoCode ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, models trained on GeoCode outperform their baselines on most benchmarks. In particular, Qwen3-VL-Instruct achieves a large improvement on OlympiadBench (+11.5), one of the most challenging geometry benchmarks, suggesting enhanced robustness on complex multi-step reasoning. Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct also shows notable gains on Geometry3K (+6.2), MathVerse (+8.4), and GeoQA (+3.8).
Overall, these results indicate that models trained on GeoCode learn transferable geometric representations and reasoning patterns, rather than overfitting to the synthetic generation distribution.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Ablation Study on Pipeline Components</h3>

<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Filtering at Different Stages of the Pipeline.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We track candidate counts at each stage to analyze the contribution of different modules.
From 264,705 randomly sampled symbolic structures, only 35,297 remain after seed selection, and 18,176 survive all subsequent stages (Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.3 Effectiveness on Test-mini and Public Benchmarks ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).
This reduction mainly reflects the removal of structurally trivial seeds that are unlikely to yield meaningful geometric relations or multi-step reasoning, rather than invalid constructions.
Seed selection is computationally lightweight and effectively prunes low-value structures early, without becoming a pipeline bottleneck.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Verification and Visualization as Quality Gates.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">On the remaining candidates, nearly half are further filtered by subsequent stages due to different failure types.
Specifically, 10,510 are rejected by semantic validation for inconsistencies among statements, reasoning traces, and answers;
4,171 fail coordinate geometric checks; 2,017 are discarded due to invalid plotting code execution;
and 423 are removed by visual quality filtering.
As a result, only 18,176 out of 35,297 (51.5%) pass all stages.
These failures correspond to distinct error modes spanning linguistic coherence, geometric validity, construction executability,
and visual clarity, indicating that the pipeline functions as a sequence of complementary quality gates rather than redundant checks.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Plotting Code Enables Stronger Visual Alignment</h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To compare different alignment supervision forms, we consider two prediction targets during SFT,
plotting code and natural-language captions of the diagram.
Captions are generated by Qwen3-VL-32B conditioned on both the rendered diagram and its plotting code.
All other inputs are kept identical, and models are trained to regress either code or captions.
Results are reported in Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.5 Plotting Code Enables Stronger Visual Alignment ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.
Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.2 Plotting Code as Explicit Alignment ‣ 3 Method ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> further shows that predicting plotting code before reasoning enables explicit reconstruction of geometric scenes,
grounding visual perception in verifiable geometric relations.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T6" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S4.T6.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">

<section id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Effectiveness of Code Alignment.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Alignment supervision improves performance over the no-alignment baseline, with plotting code yielding the most substantial gains on both Test-mini and Geometry3K, while caption-based supervision brings only marginal improvements.
Although captions and plotting code describe the same geometry, natural language is weakly structured and admits diverse surface realizations, whereas plotting code explicitly specifies constructions and spatial relations, forcing models to recover underlying geometric structure and thus providing a stronger alignment signal between vision and geometry.
We further observe that textual debiasing brings additional gains mainly when combined with code-based supervision, suggesting that debiasing strengthens visual grounding once explicit structural prediction is required.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18745v1/segment.svg" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:238/151;" width="238" height="151"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Solving accuracy and segment-level structural recovery quality on Test-mini. Samples are grouped into four equal-sized bins according to segment-level F1 between predicted and ground-truth plotting code.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Structural Recovery and Solving Performance.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To verify that the gains from code alignment arise from improved geometric perception rather than only better answer generation, we directly evaluate the structural quality of predicted plotting code on Test-mini, where ground-truth structure is available.
We measure segment-level F1 between predicted and ground-truth segments and group samples into equal-sized bins.
As shown in Fig. <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Effectiveness of Code Alignment. ‣ 4.5 Plotting Code Enables Stronger Visual Alignment ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, solving accuracy increases with higher segment-level F1, indicating that improved recovery of geometric configurations is closely associated with better reasoning performance. See Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B A Closer Look at Plotting Code as Alignment Signal ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> for further details, experiments and analysis.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present a pipeline for synthesizing multimodal geometry problems from scratch, with multi-stage validation to ensure consistency among symbolic structures, text, reasoning traces, and diagrams.
By decoupling generation into symbolic seed construction, grounded instantiation, and code-based visualization, the pipeline enables scalable synthesis of structurally complex geometry problems.
Based on this pipeline, we construct GeoCode, a high-quality dataset pairing each problem with diagrams, solutions, and plotting code, providing explicit supervision for both perception and reasoning.
Leveraging the plotting code, we further explore code prediction as an alignment strategy, which encourages models to recover underlying geometric constructions from diagrams and yields more robust visual grounding than text-based supervision, leading to improve performance across multiple geometry benchmarks.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This work aims to advance multimodal machine learning by improving visual–symbolic alignment and reasoning in geometry, a core domain for studying structured multimodal understanding. Potential positive impacts include supporting research on multimodal reasoning, enabling better educational tools for geometry learning, and facilitating future studies on interpretable visual–symbolic models.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Sx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">All data used in this work are synthetically generated through automated symbolic and geometric procedures, and do not involve personal data, sensitive content, or real-world imagery, thereby posing no privacy or data protection concerns.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Sx1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As with many advances in reasoning-capable language and vision–language models, there is a general risk that improved problem-solving abilities could be misused for academic dishonesty or automated answer generation. However, this risk is not specific to our method and is shared by most progress in large-scale reasoning models. We believe that the primary and intended use of our work is to support research and education, and we do not foresee significant negative societal consequences specific to this contribution.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Discussion</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we compare our approach with existing methods and discuss future directions. Our work focuses on synthesizing multimodal geometry data and enabling effective visual alignment. We first examine related data synthesis methods, then highlight our core innovations, and finally outline promising future directions.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Comparison with Existing Data Synthesis Methods.</h5>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Early data synthesis approaches for geometry reasoning primarily focused on augmenting existing datasets rather than generating new visual content. G-LLaVA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite> represents one of the earliest data synthesis methods in this domain, but it does not generate new images; instead, it augments datasets through semantic modifications and explores text-based visual geometric alignment using predicate-based methods. Subsequent works have advanced toward generating novel images. R-CoT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite> employs a sampling-based approach to select geometric configurations and synthesizes geometry data using large language models. GeoGen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite> leverages the symbolic engine FormalGeo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite> to search in symbolic space and translates results using LLMs. TrustGeoGen <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite> represents a particularly powerful approach that exclusively searches in symbolic space using the AlphaGeometry engine to synthesize data. MathCoder-VL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> introduces an interesting variation by adjusting temperature parameters to generate novel figures through code, synthesizing instruction pairs using LLMs, and validating correctness through A/B testing. We acknowledge the valuable insights these works have provided for our research.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Compared to these approaches, our method introduces several core innovations. <em id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">First</em>, we decompose the synthesis process into three distinct stages, factorizing geometry into basic structure, instance information, and visualization code. This decomposition is not only more intuitive but has also proven more effective in practice, enabling the generation of more diverse structures and leveraging LLM priors to produce interesting problems. From this perspective, our approach differs fundamentally from the aforementioned works. <em id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Second</em>, code-based visualization provides complete geometric information, allowing us to thoroughly explore the role of visual modalities. Through debiasing and explicit alignment methods, we promote visual understanding, representing a deeper investigation beyond synthesis. Unlike G-LLaVA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>, MAVIS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>, and EAGLE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>, which employ different alignment strategies, our approach uses plotting code for alignment, which we empirically demonstrate to be more effective. <em id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Third</em>, we acknowledge that LLM hallucinations pose challenges for synthesizing mathematical problems, necessitating multiple validation mechanisms. Therefore, we implement multi-level verification through semantic, numerical, and visual checks to ensure the correctness of multimodal problems. In particular, our code-based verification represents a significant step forward in synthesizing mathematical geometry problems.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Future Directions.</h5>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Looking ahead, we believe that data synthesis methods will inspire more downstream tasks, particularly in areas such as Thinking With Images, enabling more effective supervision or reinforcement learning algorithm development. However, data synthesis represents only the first step. We also hope that code-based alignment approaches can find broader applications, where explicit structural grounding can bridge the gap between visual perception and symbolic reasoning.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="A1.F6.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18745v1/B.svg" id="A1.F6.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/394;" width="476" height="394"></object>

</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
