</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>A Closer Look at Plotting Code as Alignment Signal</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As demonstrated in Section <a href="#S4.SS5" title="4.5 Plotting Code Enables Stronger Visual Alignment ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.5</span></a>, code-based alignment supervision yields substantial improvements over caption-based or no-alignment baselines. In this appendix, we provide a closer diagnostic analysis to clarify <em id="A2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">what</em> the model learns from plotting-code supervision. In particular, we aim to distinguish two plausible explanations: (i) the model mainly benefits from learning a rigid output format (i.e., producing well-formed code), or (ii) the model truly improves its ability to reconstruct geometric structure from the diagram, which subsequently supports correct reasoning.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Segment-Level Structural F1: Definition and Motivation.</h5>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To directly probe structural understanding beyond final answers, we introduce segment-level F1 as a geometry-aware evaluation metric on Test-mini, where ground-truth plotting code is available. The key idea is simple: if a model genuinely “sees” the diagram structure, it should be able to recover the correct set of segments (edges) that define the core relational skeleton of the construction. We focus on segments because they provide a stable and nearly canonical representation of structure. A segment is uniquely identified by an unordered pair of endpoints. Concretely, for each instance we extract the segment set from predicted plotting code and ground-truth plotting code, denoted as <math id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{\text{pred}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mtext>pred</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{\text{pred}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{\text{gt}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mtext>gt</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{\text{gt}}</annotation></semantics></math>, where each segment is represented as an unordered endpoint pair. We compute precision, recall, and F1 by:</p>
<table id="A2.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A2.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle P</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A2.E1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{|S_{\text{pred}}\cap S_{\text{gt}}|}{|S_{\text{pred}}|},\quad R=\frac{|S_{\text{pred}}\cap S_{\text{gt}}|}{|S_{\text{gt}}|}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mtext>pred</mtext></msub><mo>∩</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mtext>gt</mtext></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mtext>pred</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mtext>pred</mtext></msub><mo>∩</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mtext>gt</mtext></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mtext>gt</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{|S_{\text{pred}}\cap S_{\text{gt}}|}{|S_{\text{pred}}|},\quad R=\frac{|S_{\text{pred}}\cap S_{\text{gt}}|}{|S_{\text{gt}}|},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="A2.E2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><span id="A2.E2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath">F1</span></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A2.E2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{2PR}{P+R}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{2PR}{P+R}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">We then rank all Test-mini samples by their segment-level F1 and split them into four equal-sized groups (quartiles). The main-text result (Fig. <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Effectiveness of Code Alignment. ‣ 4.5 Plotting Code Enables Stronger Visual Alignment ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>) shows a clear monotonic trend: higher segment-level F1 is consistently associated with higher solving accuracy. Importantly, this metric is <em id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">structural</em> rather than outcome-driven: it evaluates whether the predicted code recovers the correct geometric relations encoded by the diagram, independent of how the model verbalizes its reasoning or formats its final answer. Therefore, the positive correlation provides direct evidence that the gains from plotting-code supervision are tied to improved structural reconstruction ability.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Parsing Is Not the Bottleneck.</h5>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A natural concern is that plotting code might mainly help because it enforces a strict output template, and the observed gains could simply reflect “format learning” rather than better geometry understanding. To test this hypothesis, we examine the relationship between parsing success and solving accuracy (Fig. <a href="#A1.F6.sf1" title="Figure 6(a) ‣ Figure 6 ‣ Future Directions. ‣ Appendix A Discussion ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6(a)</span></a>). On Test-mini, the model achieves a high parsing success rate: <math id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="219" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>219</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">219</annotation></semantics></math> cases are parsable, corresponding to <math id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="81.7\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>81.7</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">81.7\%</annotation></semantics></math> successful parsing. This already indicates that the surface format of plotting code is learned relatively quickly. However, parsing success itself shows little explanatory power for downstream problem solving. Among the parsable cases, <math id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="83/219" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>83</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>219</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">83/219</annotation></semantics></math> are solved correctly (<math id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="37.9\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>37.9</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">37.9\%</annotation></semantics></math>). Among the <math id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="49" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>49</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">49</annotation></semantics></math> non-parsable cases, <math id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="18/49" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>18</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>49</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">18/49</annotation></semantics></math> are solved correctly (<math id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="36.7\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>36.7</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">36.7\%</annotation></semantics></math>). The accuracy difference is negligible, suggesting that syntactic well-formedness or executability is not the key factor determining whether the model can solve the problem. In other words, the model can often answer correctly even when its code cannot be parsed, and conversely, it can still fail even when it produces well-formed code. This observation strongly argues against the “format-only” explanation: the improvement from code supervision cannot be reduced to merely learning how to emit a JSON-like structure.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Why Annotations Matter.</h5>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If formatting is not the driver, what aspect of plotting code is most predictive of reasoning success? We further analyze a structure-critical component: geometric annotations (e.g., right angles, lengths, and other marked constraints), which are known to be decisive in classical geometry problem solving because they specify the nontrivial constraints that reasoning must operate on. We focus on the <math id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="189" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>189</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">189</annotation></semantics></math> Test-mini instances that contain explicit annotations and manually assess whether the predicted annotation is structurally correct (fully correct vs. partially/fully incorrect). The results (Fig. <a href="#A1.F6.sf2" title="Figure 6(b) ‣ Figure 6 ‣ Future Directions. ‣ Appendix A Discussion ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6(b)</span></a>) reveal a strong dependence on annotation fidelity. When the predicted annotation is fully correct, solving accuracy reaches <math id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="43/84=51.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>43</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>84</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>51.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">43/84=51.2\%</annotation></semantics></math>. When the annotation is partially or fully incorrect, accuracy drops sharply to <math id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16/105=15.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>105</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>15.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16/105=15.2\%</annotation></semantics></math>. This gap is substantial and qualitatively different from the parsing analysis above. It indicates that recovering the <em id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">right constraints</em>—not merely producing a valid container—plays a central role in enabling correct reasoning. Conceptually, this is exactly what we expect from geometry: annotations act as “hard facts” that anchor the deductive process. A small structural mistake (e.g., missing a right angle or mis-assigning an equality) can invalidate the entire reasoning chain, even if all other parts of the diagram are correctly recognized. Therefore, annotation correctness provides a more faithful diagnostic for geometric understanding than format validity.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Summary.</h5>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Taken together, these analyses paint a consistent picture of how plotting code functions as an alignment signal. Segment-level F1 demonstrates that better structural recovery of segments is tightly associated with higher solving accuracy, supporting the claim that code supervision strengthens geometric perception and structure reconstruction. The parsing analysis further rules out a superficial explanation: models can quickly learn the plotting-code format (high parsing success), yet format validity alone has little correlation with whether problems are solved correctly. In contrast, annotation correctness shows a strong and practically meaningful relationship with solving performance, highlighting that what truly matters is faithful recovery of geometric constraints and relations. Overall, these results support our central conclusion: plotting-code supervision improves multimodal geometry reasoning not by enforcing a rigid output template, but by explicitly training models to reconstruct diagram structure—especially constraint-bearing relations—thereby providing a reliable internal representation that downstream reasoning can build upon.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Training and Evaluation Details</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section provides detailed specifications of our training and evaluation procedures, including supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with GRPO.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Supervised Fine-Tuning</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We perform SFT using cross-entropy loss on our synthetic geometry dataset. The training configuration is as follows:</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Model Configuration.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-7B-Instruct as base models, both following identical training configurations. The vision tower is frozen during training, while the multi-modal projector and language model are fine-tuned. We employ LoRA with rank 128, applied to all trainable parameters. The maximum image resolution is set to <math id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="512\times 512" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>512</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>512</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">512\times 512</annotation></semantics></math> pixels (262,144 total pixels).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Training Hyperparameters.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The model is trained for 2 epochs with a learning rate of <math id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0\times 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math> using cosine learning rate scheduling. We use a warmup ratio of 0.1, batch size of 4 per device with gradient accumulation over 8 steps (effective batch size of 32), and bfloat16 precision. The maximum sequence length is set to 8192 tokens. We train on 18k samples from our synthetic dataset.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Loss Function.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">During SFT, we minimize the standard cross-entropy loss:</p>
<table id="A3.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log P(y_{t}\mid y_{&lt;t},x,I)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>SFT</mtext></msub><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.055em">−</mo><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></munderover><mi>log</mi><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log P(y_{t}\mid y_{&lt;t},x,I),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> is the input text prompt, <math id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>I</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I</annotation></semantics></math> is the input image, <math id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the token at position <math id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> is the total sequence length. The model is supervised to predict plotting code, reasoning traces, and final answers.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Reinforcement Learning with GRPO</h3>

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After SFT, we further optimize the model using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>, a variant of PPO that groups multiple responses for more stable policy updates.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">GRPO Objective.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The GRPO objective function is defined as:</p>
<table id="A3.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{GRPO}}=\mathbb{E}_{(x,I)\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{g=1}^{G}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{g}}\left(r(x,I,y_{g,i})-\bar{r}_{g}\right)\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{g,i}\mid x,I)-\beta\text{KL}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}})\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>[</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>G</mi></mfrac><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>G</mi></munderover><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi></msub></munderover><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>g</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.167em">)</mo></mrow><mi>log</mi><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>β</mi><mtext>KL</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{GRPO}}=\mathbb{E}_{(x,I)\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{g=1}^{G}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{g}}\left(r(x,I,y_{g,i})-\bar{r}_{g}\right)\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{g,i}\mid x,I)-\beta\text{KL}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}})\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of groups, <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{g}</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of responses in group <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r(x,I,y_{g,i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r(x,I,y_{g,i})</annotation></semantics></math> is the reward for response <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{g,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{g,i}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{r}_{g}=\frac{1}{n_{g}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{g}}r(x,I,y_{g,i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>g</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi></msub></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>g</mi></msub></msubsup><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{r}_{g}=\frac{1}{n_{g}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{g}}r(x,I,y_{g,i})</annotation></semantics></math> is the group mean reward, <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> is the current policy, <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\text{ref}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mtext>ref</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\text{ref}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the reference policy (the SFT model), and <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.01</annotation></semantics></math> is the KL penalty coefficient.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Reward Function.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We employ a composite reward function that combines format correctness and answer accuracy:</p>
<table id="A3.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r(x,I,y)=r_{\text{format}}(y)+r_{\text{answer}}(x,I,y)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>format</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>answer</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r(x,I,y)=r_{\text{format}}(y)+r_{\text{answer}}(x,I,y),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\text{format}}(y)\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>format</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\text{format}}(y)\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> is a binary reward for correct output format, and <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\text{answer}}(x,I,y)\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>answer</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\text{answer}}(x,I,y)\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> is a binary reward for answer correctness.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The format reward <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\text{format}}(y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>format</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\text{format}}(y)</annotation></semantics></math> requires the model output to follow the structure with three explicitly delimited blocks:</p>
<table id="A3.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\texttt{&lt;code&gt;}\penalty\ C\penalty\ \texttt{&lt;/code&gt;}\penalty\ \texttt{&lt;think&gt;}\penalty\ R\penalty\ \texttt{&lt;/think&gt;}\penalty\ \texttt{&lt;answer&gt;}\penalty\ A\penalty\ \texttt{&lt;/answer&gt;}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">&lt;code&gt;</mtext><mo lspace="0.500em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0.500em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">&lt;/code&gt;</mtext><mo lspace="0.500em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">&lt;think&gt;</mtext><mo lspace="0.500em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0.500em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">&lt;/think&gt;</mtext><mo lspace="0.500em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">&lt;answer&gt;</mtext><mo lspace="0.500em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0.500em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">&lt;/answer&gt;</mtext></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{&lt;code&gt;}\penalty\ C\penalty\ \texttt{&lt;/code&gt;}\penalty\ \texttt{&lt;think&gt;}\penalty\ R\penalty\ \texttt{&lt;/think&gt;}\penalty\ \texttt{&lt;answer&gt;}\penalty\ A\penalty\ \texttt{&lt;/answer&gt;},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> is the plotting code, <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> is the reasoning trace (placed inside <span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;think&gt;</span> <span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;/think&gt;</span>), and <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> is the final answer (placed inside <span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;answer&gt;</span> <span id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;/answer&gt;</span>). The format reward is 1 if the output contains all three required components in the correct order with correct opening and closing tags, and 0 otherwise.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The answer reward <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\text{answer}}(x,I,y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>answer</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\text{answer}}(x,I,y)</annotation></semantics></math> is 1 if the extracted answer <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> matches the ground truth answer (with numerical tolerance for floating-point comparisons), and 0 otherwise.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Training Configuration.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train for 1 epoch with a learning rate of <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5.0\times 10^{-6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.0\times 10^{-6}</annotation></semantics></math>. The training batch size is 256, with PPO mini-batch size of 128 and micro-batch size of 8 per GPU. We sample <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=4</annotation></semantics></math> responses per prompt for reward estimation. The KL loss uses the low-variance KL estimator with coefficient <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.01</annotation></semantics></math>, and the clip ratio is set to <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=0.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=0.2</annotation></semantics></math>. We use FSDP (Fully Sharded Data Parallel) for distributed training across 4 H200 GPUs, with gradient checkpointing enabled to reduce memory usage.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Implementation Details.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The rollout and reference models use tensor model parallelism with size 2. The rollout engine uses vLLM with GPU memory utilization set to 0.6. We disable the multi-modal preprocessor cache and use eager execution mode. The maximum prompt and response lengths are both set to 2048 tokens.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.3 </span>Evaluation Protocol</h3>

<section id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Test Set Construction.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For non-geometry-specific datasets, we follow the original dataset annotations and select subsets that involve plane geometry problems. Table <a href="#A3.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Test Set Construction. ‣ C.3 Evaluation Protocol ‣ Appendix C Training and Evaluation Details ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> summarizes the sizes of these geometry-focused minisets extracted from each benchmark.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evaluation Details.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure fair and consistent evaluation across all models, we adopt a standardized evaluation protocol. We set the temperature parameter <math id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0</annotation></semantics></math> for all evaluations, enabling deterministic greedy decoding. All models use the same system prompt: <span id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">You are a mathematical reasoning assistant.
<br class="ltx_break">Your task is to solve the problem and give the correct answer.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For answer extraction and matching, we parse answers from either <span id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;answer&gt;</span> or <span id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;box&gt;</span> tags in the model output. We then process the extracted answers through LaTeX parsing and symbolic evaluation using SymPy to compute numerical values. An answer is considered correct if the computed value matches the ground truth answer within a tolerance of <math id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-6}</annotation></semantics></math>. This numerical matching approach ensures robust evaluation across different answer formats and representations.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To maintain fairness, all models are evaluated using identical evaluation procedures, including the same answer extraction logic, parsing methods, and matching criteria. We evaluate only problems that require solution generation (i.e., solution-type problems), excluding other problem types from the evaluation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Effect of Backbone Models</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">By constructing hard and structurally complex geometry instances that require multi-step reasoning and sophisticated spatial understanding, our method provides a natural testbed for evaluating how different vision-language backbones respond to reinforcement learning optimization. We compare Qwen2.5-VL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite> and Qwen3-VL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite> under identical GRPO training configurations, examining both their final performance on Test-mini (Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Complexity. ‣ 4.2 Quality and Difficulty of GeoCode ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) and their training dynamics through reward curves (Figure <a href="#A4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ Appendix D Effect of Backbone Models ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.F7" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18745v1/curve1.svg" id="A4.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:229/136;" width="229" height="136"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18745v1/curve2.svg" id="A4.F7.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:229/136;" width="229" height="136"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A4.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="A4.F7.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">GRPO reward curves for different backbones.<span id="A4.F7.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Qwen2.5-VL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite> (left) exhibits slower reward growth with larger fluctuations, while Qwen3-VL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite> (right) shows a more stable and monotonic improvement, indicating stronger geometric reasoning ability and better alignment with our hard, structurally complex data.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The results reveal a clear distinction between the two backbones. Qwen3-VL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>, which has been extensively pre-trained on STEM and geometry-related corpora, demonstrates superior geometric reasoning capabilities: during GRPO training, its average reward exhibits steady, monotonic growth and converges to a high, stable plateau (Figure <a href="#A4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ Appendix D Effect of Backbone Models ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, right). This behavior suggests that Qwen3-VL can effectively leverage the structural complexity and difficulty of our generated data to drive consistent policy improvement. In contrast, while Qwen2.5-VL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite> also benefits from GRPO and achieves notable gains (from 13.1% to 20.5% on Test-mini), its reward curve displays slower growth and significantly larger variance throughout training (Figure <a href="#A4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ Appendix D Effect of Backbone Models ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, left), indicating less stable optimization and lower sample efficiency.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This comparison yields two important insights. First, backbone selection is critical for vertical domains like geometry, where specialized pre-training on domain-relevant data substantially facilitates downstream reinforcement learning. Second, the high difficulty and structural richness of our automatically generated data serve as an effective probe that can distinguish between strong backbones, validating both the quality of our data generation pipeline and its utility for benchmarking geometric reasoning capabilities.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Extensibility of Our Pipeline</h2>

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our generation pipeline is divided into three stages: symbolic seed generation, instance instantiation, and visualization. The first stage lays down the underlying geometric structure, while the latter two stages materialize concrete problem instances and diagrams. This modular design naturally raises the question of whether the pipeline can be extended to <em id="A5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">ingest</em> existing textual problems and synthesize new data that reduces the domain gap between our synthetic distribution and established benchmarks.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To explore this direction, we examine common geometry datasets in the community. Geometry3K provides relatively sparse textual descriptions, which often lack sufficient structural information to serve as reliable seeds for our symbolic generator. In contrast, GeoQA contains rich and highly structured textual statements that implicitly encode geometric configurations and reasoning chains, for example: “In quadrilateral <math id="A5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ABCD" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ABCD</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\angle B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∠</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\angle B</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="A5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="40^{\circ}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>40</mn><mo>∘</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40^{\circ}</annotation></semantics></math> larger than <math id="A5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\angle A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∠</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\angle A</annotation></semantics></math>; what is the measure of <math id="A5.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\angle D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∠</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\angle D</annotation></semantics></math>?” or “In <math id="A5.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\triangle ABC" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">△</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\triangle ABC</annotation></semantics></math>, points <math id="A5.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A5.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math> lie on <math id="A5.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="AB" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">AB</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A5.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="AC" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">AC</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="A5.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="DE\parallel BC" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow><mo fence="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">DE\parallel BC</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A5.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{AD}{AB}=\frac{3}{7}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>7</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{AD}{AB}=\frac{3}{7}</annotation></semantics></math>; given <math id="A5.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="AE=6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">AE=6</annotation></semantics></math>, what is the length of <math id="A5.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="EC" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">EC</annotation></semantics></math>?” These formulations clearly expose the roles of key entities and constraints, making them suitable as structural backbones.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by this observation, we propose an extended pipeline where we reuse the textual stems of existing training problems as high-level structural seeds, and then apply our instantiation and visualization stages to generate variants with concrete coordinates and diagrams. This “text-to-structure” augmentation bridges part of the domain gap by aligning the combinatorial structure of our synthetic data with that of real benchmarks, while still benefiting from automatic validation and visualization.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate this approach in an out-of-distribution (OOD) setting on GeoQA, comparing three training regimes: (i) <em id="A5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Baseline</em>, using only the original pretrained backbones; (ii) <em id="A5.p4.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">OOD</em>, training on our original synthetic dataset; and (iii) <em id="A5.p4.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Ours</em>, further augmenting training with text-seeded synthetic data derived from GeoQA-style problems. Results are summarized in Table <a href="#A5.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ Appendix E Extensibility of Our Pipeline ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.T8" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A5.T8.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="A5.T8.3.1" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="A5.T8.3.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:7.0pt;padding-right:7.0pt;"><span id="A5.T8.3.1.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">OOD</span></td>

</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 8: </span><span id="A5.T8.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Extending our pipeline with text-seeded synthetic data on GeoQA.</span> “Baseline” denotes the original pretrained backbones, “OOD” denotes training only on our synthetic dataset, and “Ours” further augments training with data synthesized by feeding real textual problem statements into our instantiation and visualization stages. The extended pipeline yields consistent gains for both backbones, indicating that our method can effectively adapt to existing geometry corpora and narrow the domain gap.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A5.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, these results demonstrate that our solver-driven pipeline is not limited to fully synthetic symbolic seeds, but can flexibly absorb real-world textual problems as structural inputs. This extensibility enables principled adaptation to diverse geometry datasets and provides a general recipe for combining symbolic generation with existing benchmarks.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18745v1/predicte.svg" id="A5.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/153;" width="476" height="153"></object>

</figure>
</section>
<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Example Data from Our Pipeline</h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section presents example diagrams generated by our pipeline to illustrate the types of geometric structures it produces.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A5.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Appendix E Extensibility of Our Pipeline ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> provides statistical insights into the predicate distribution of our generated problems. The left panel shows the frequency distribution of predicates sampled during seed generation, revealing a long-tail distribution where commonly used predicates such as perpendicularity and parallelism occur with much higher probability than less frequent ones like concyclic or similarity relations. This distribution pattern demonstrates that our generation process is not a rigid template-based procedure, but rather a flexible process that naturally captures the varying frequencies of different geometric relationships in real-world problems. The right panel displays the distribution of predicate counts per problem, which follows an approximately normal distribution centered around a mean of 10 predicates. This level of structural complexity, with an average of 10 geometric constraints per problem, significantly exceeds the complexity typically found in existing geometry datasets, as can be observed in the detailed examples shown in Figure <a href="#A6.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ Appendix F Example Data from Our Pipeline ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A6.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ Appendix F Example Data from Our Pipeline ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> shows 20 example diagrams from our fully synthetic dataset, while Figure <a href="#A6.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ Appendix F Example Data from Our Pipeline ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> displays 20 example diagrams generated using the extended approach described in Appendix  <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Extensibility of Our Pipeline ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>(text-seeded synthesis).</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F9" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18745v1/ours.png" id="A6.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/562;" width="476" height="562" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A6.F9.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 9</span>: </span><span id="A6.F9.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Example diagrams from our fully synthetic pipeline.<span id="A6.F9.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> These 20 examples illustrate the geometric structures generated by our solver-driven pipeline, featuring dense relational constraints, multi-step constructions, and non-trivial geometric configurations. Each diagram exhibits rich structural complexity with multiple geometric entities, intricate spatial relationships, and sophisticated reasoning patterns.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A6.F10" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18745v1/sythesis.png" id="A6.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/562;" width="476" height="562" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A6.F10.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 10</span>: </span><span id="A6.F10.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Example diagrams from text-seeded synthesis (Appendix E).<span id="A6.F10.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> These 20 examples illustrate the geometric structures generated by feeding existing textual problem statements into our instantiation and visualization stages.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A6.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The diagrams in Figure <a href="#A6.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ Appendix F Example Data from Our Pipeline ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> demonstrate the complex geometric structures that our fully synthetic pipeline can generate. These examples showcase several key characteristics of our solver-driven generation approach. First, the diagrams exhibit <span id="A6.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">dense geometric constructions</span> with multiple overlapping circles, intricate polygon configurations, and complex intersection patterns that require sophisticated spatial reasoning to fully comprehend. Second, they feature <span id="A6.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">non-trivial relational constraints</span> including rich networks of geometric relations such as parallelism, perpendicularity, cyclic quadrilaterals, similarity constructions, and congruence relations that create multi-step reasoning chains. Third, the problems involve <span id="A6.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">high entity density</span> with numerous points, segments, and circles that have interwoven dependencies, challenging both visual perception and symbolic reasoning capabilities. The structural richness of these diagrams reflects the effectiveness of our pipeline in exploring complex geometric configurations through symbolic seed generation, dependency construction, and rigorous verification mechanisms.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The diagrams in Figure <a href="#A6.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ Appendix F Example Data from Our Pipeline ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> illustrate the output of our extended pipeline when applied to existing textual problem formulations. These examples demonstrate the compatibility and extensibility of our framework, showing that the instantiation and visualization stages can effectively process different types of input sources. By feeding textual problem statements into our pipeline, we can leverage the same verification mechanisms and visualization capabilities to produce geometrically consistent diagrams, even when the underlying structural seeds originate from existing problem formulations rather than purely symbolic generation. This flexibility highlights the modular design of our pipeline, where the instantiation and visualization components can operate independently of the seed generation stage, enabling adaptation to diverse data sources while maintaining strict geometric correctness and visual quality standards.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Together, these example diagrams illustrate the range of geometric structures that our pipeline can produce, from complex solver-driven constructions to text-grounded instantiations, demonstrating both the effectiveness of our fully synthetic approach and the compatibility of our framework with alternative input modalities.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Detailed Pipeline and Algorithms</h2>

<div id="A7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our complete generation pipeline is summarized in <a href="#algorithm1" title="In Appendix G Detailed Pipeline and Algorithms ‣ Synthesizing Multimodal Geometry Datasets from Scratch and Enabling Visual Alignment via Plotting Code" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Algorithm</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. In this section, we provide detailed descriptions of the coordinate verification mechanism, which ensures geometric consistency between symbolic constraints, numerical coordinates, and visual diagrams.</p>
</div>
